verses.en: V. 1. בראשית ברא אלקים. The phonetic relation of ראש to רעש and רחש of which the one designates a physical movement and the other an internal one, teaches that we are to consider ראש as the seat of movement, as that organ from which all external and internal movement has its origin. Hence ראשית means the beginning of a movement, a beginning in time, never in space. A beginning in space is called, like its end, קצה, for they are both extremities, which, according to the way one looks at them, may be considered the beginning or the end. So that בראשית וגו׳ means: in the beginning of all coming into existence, it was God Who created, or taking it in connection with the two objects that follow: At the very beginning God created the heaven and the earth. In any case בראשית expresses the fact that nothing preceded God’s creation, that heaven and earth came into existence solely by the creation of God. This affirms creation out of nothing יש מאין, a fact that forms the foundation-stone of the understanding which God’s Torah wishes to build up in us. The contrary belief, that matter always existed, and only ascribes to the Creator a formative function, which is equally the foundation stone of heathen conception up to this very day is not only a methaphysical lie which has robbed the theories of mankind as to the origin of the world of the truth i.e. of agreement with actuality, but is the much farther-reaching pernicious denial of all freedom of will in God and Man, which undermines all morality. If the material was there, was given to the world-framer, He could only make the best possible out of that material but not the absolute best world. All physical and moral evil would then unavoidably lie in the imperfection of the material. God Himself could not save the world from either physical or moral evil. Man could as little be master of his body as God of the material of the world. Freedom would be absent from the world. Blind pitiless necessity would rule the world together with its God and its men. The first word of the Teaching of God, of which in truth it can be said: פתח דבריך יאיר (Ps. 119,130), dispels at once this comfortless conception of God, the world, and mankind. “בראשית ברא אלקים״! Hereby all that follows stands or falls. Everything, all material, all forms, everything existing, has sprung from the completely free, all-mighty creative Will of God. Still, to-day, the Creator rules completely freely over the material and form of all creatures, over the forces that work in matter, over the laws that govern that working, and over the resulting forms, for it is His free almighty Will that created the matter, that embodied the forces which work within it, and it is His Law which governs the result. And as He ruled free-willed over His world, He could invest Man, in whom He had breathed a spark of His Own free-willed nature, by this spark, with free will over his small world; free-willed disposition of his body and its forces, and could place him to be a free-willed likeness of the Free-willed God, in the world governed by His Almight. The בראשית of the world created by God is not the best possible, but the actual best. With all its seeming evils, it corresponds to the plans of the Wisdom of its Creator Who could have created it otherwise if such had been more in accordance with His Will. Man created by God at בראשית, has, with all his moral imperfections, the ability to be adequate, in the highest degree of moral perfection, to the moral ideal set before him by his Creator. The possibility of his failing to do so, itself is part of his moral completion, more, it is the fundamental condition for his moral freedom of will. Both, the world and Man will achieve the highest goal of goodness for which both were created, for the God Who has placed this goal before them created them, by His Almighty absolutely unhindered free Will, for this goal. He would have created them otherwise if this would have been more conductive to the goal He had set out of His Own Free-Will. This is a fact that we constantly call ever afresh to our minds in קדיש, in which we express the conviction that His Great Name will surely win “recognition and sanctification in a world די ברא כרעותיה, which He had created just for this end, entirely according to His Will”. In this sense too, we can understand the sayings of our sages: חלה מעשר ובכורים נברא עולם בזכות ישראל ,בזכות משה, בזכות which are all called ראשית or ובורא העולם הקב״ה היה מביט בתורה. If Israel and Moses appear as quite a new beginning of a quite new phase of the development of history, and hence are called ראשית, or they deserve the name as being the first beginning of the realisation of the ideal set with the creation of Man, as being the first fruits of God’s harvest: if חלה, מעשר, בכורים are nought but expressions of acknowledging return-gifts of the world to its Giver; if, above all, the Torah is the first building-stone for the purpose which God had in creating the world, and out of which that purpose is to be achieved, and therefore is called ראשית; then all these ends, even if only developed later, must have been ensured right at the beginning of the world, just because the world was created בראשית, came into existence completely out of God’s Hands, so that from its very inception it was formed for these high purposes. “God”, it says, “looked into the Torah and created the world accordingly”. So that in this we see the cornerstone of our awareness of God and the world, and when this awareness had disappeared and was to be established afresh, we can understand the free-willed, unlimited sway of God over the world had to be proved by miracles. These, as נסים, banners held aloft as directing and guiding signs, were to lead us back to regaining the consciousness of the free, completely unhindered Almight of God, a consciousness which as we have indicated forms the preliminary condition for all Man’s consciousness of morality, accordingly, the preliminary condition for our whole relation to the תורה.

ברא. The cognate roots פרע ,פרא ,פרח ,ברה ,ברח which all have the meaning of striving to get out, or getting out of a state of being constrained or bound, give ברא the underlying conception of bringing something out into the open; in Chaldean too, ברא means quite simply, outside. So that ברא means bringing something into reality which hitherto had only existed inwardly, in the mind. It is creating something purely out of one’s mind and will and out of nothing else. It is the real יש מאין, and is accordingly only used for creation by God. Before the world existed materially it existed only as a thought — to speak in terms of human beings — in the mind of the Creator. The act of creation gave this thought an external concrete existence. The whole world, in toto and in detail, is accordingly nothing but a materialised thought of God. An idea that we shall meet again when we come to consider the root היה, the Jewish conception of being (v. 2). (The use of ברא to designate being plump, corpulent and healthy also comes from this meaning of the root of becoming visible, concrete, tangible, and from that we get בריה ,ברה and ברית to designate the first meal, breakfast, a snack which refreshes a person, makes him feel strong again. Also ובראת לך שם ,ובראתו (Josh. 17,15, 18) would mean, make room there that you can spread out.

אלקים. The root אלה occurs in the demonstrative pronoun אלה “these” But the demonstrative plural “these” always looks at a plurality of things as being in some way joined together to form a unit. And so, whereas אלה in general points to the visible plurality of objects in the world, the name of God אלוה could designate the One Whose might and will encompasses all these objects together in unity. The One through Whom all the plurality, by everything being related to Him, becomes one union, one whole, one world. Hence אלוה really means: the One Who is ruler, director, law-giver, judge of the world, מדת הדין. Hence the human rulers, directors, law-givers, judges of people of the little human world are also called אלהים. To the heathen, the world altogether fell into many groups of phenomena and spheres, each of which had its own special ruler to whom were attributed special powers. This was the natural result of the fundamental error, referred to above, of considering matter as having been always in existence and the consequent lack of freedom of the world-creating God-head, Who, accordingly sank to the unfree character of a force of nature, which could not produce objects which were in direct opposition to one another, or fundamentally differing phenomena. A world full of such opposing and differing phenomena must accordingly have behind it as many god-heads, as many אלהים as there are groups of such phenomena. Judaism takes the whole plentitude of power of these supposedly numerous אלהים and attributes it exclusively to the One Unique God, by calling Him אלקים. Even just this uniting all these heathen separated attributes of power in One God, raises this One God of Judaism high above the conception of a mere force of nature, as it is only out of a completely free Almighty Will that the most widely opposing elements could be united together for the purpose of One Director of a world so full of differing phenomena. Using a plural form to designate a plentitude of powers combined in one person is moreover by no means unusual in expressions of mastery and power in the Hebrew language, such as בעלים ,אדנים. They always designate a person who possesses the various powers which rule over any object, to whom, accordingly, this object is completely subjected in every direction. From this underlying conception of the root אלה as world-director, law-giver, judge, the same root is also used to designate an oath אלה. An oath, according to the Jewish idea, is not merely an appellation to the God-head, but is an actual placing of the whole of the material world of the one who swears under the verdict of the One Who has power to deal with them (a way of regarding an oath that is likewise expressed by the word השבע, see Jeshurun V.p.19), and the curse by which the destroying power of the Director of the world will proclaim the falsity of a false oath. יחדו נאלחו ,נתעב ונאלח (Ps. 14,3), — אלח is probably only a strong form of אלה and in the Niphal it means: to be under the curse. — Significant is the remark of our sages that it does not say ברא בראשית אלקים, but בראשית ברא אלקים. In the way we have believed this name of God to be derived from אלה, God can be called אלקים only after the creation of the world, as it refers to His relation to the world. But the way it puts it, it means: the God in Whom we now all see as the Director of the World, it is He, too, out of Whose Almighty Will this world first sprang forth.

את from the root אות, as is evident from אותי אותך etc. אות related to אוד .אוד a handle, a lever, the means by which an action is accomplished, hence אוד a fire-rake, a piece of wood with which to stir the fire. אודות, the causes, hence על אודות. Hence perhaps איד the bringer-about of the rain, the moisture that rises up from the earth. אות the means for making something known, a sign, that is not the thing itself but leads to it. But this is then at once the particle of the accusative את which presents the object in all those phases that represent its characteristics, its effect and relationship by which its nature is to be recognised, which accordingly are its sign, the means by which it gets known. It is a deeply distinctive character of the thought that lies behind the Jewish language that את is used only for the accusative, the object, but never for the nominative, the subject. It is how the object appears with regard to something else, the subject. But the real nature of things is completely veiled, incomprehensible to anybody or anything else. We only know things by their אותות, in their effect and doings by which they show their characteristics, and which form the sole means by which they can be known. So that our sages, in their deep understanding of the language, find a significant difference if the object is expressed simply by its name or if by means of את. In the former case the effect extends to the object alone, in the latter to all those factors by which its essential effect shows itself. Thus כבד אביך would make only the father the object of the honouring, כבד את אביך extends this honouring to all those who stand in such a relation to the father that the personality of the father is represented in them e.g. אשת אביך the stepmother, and equally so, אמך את includes the stepfather. So that really את is a רבוי, that allows the object to be taken in wider sense. So, here, too the את extends the conception שמים to include all the heavenly bodies, and the ארץ to include all that is on earth, which are just the effects which heaven and earth characteristically imprint on us.

את השמים ואת הארץ. We have already — in Jeshurun vol. VIII p.274 et seq. — tried to develop the conception שמים and ארץ from the roots of the words. We found שמים to be the designation of the whole extra-terristrial world, as the double שם, as the above and below, “there”, the immeasurable “double” space, above and beneath the earth, or rather — from the root שום, directing, fixing the place — as the whole complex of extra-terrestrial bodies through whose mutually attracting and repelling forces the earth, like every other point in the universe, keeps to its appointed place. For every point in the universe, the whole of the rest of space with all its bodies, would be שמים. In any case the word שמים already tells us that we have not to expect here any superterrestrial cosmogonic revelations. The extra-terrestrial world is only mentioned and considered in its relation to the earth. The תורה wishes to be the Word of God, our signpost on earth and the means of finding our bearings here in our earthly world. These, and to teach us to think of ourselves as having come from God, are its purposes. That is why it places us in front of Our heaven and Our earth, and says: ואת הארץ את השמים, this heaven with all its countless stars, and this earth with its countless creatures, the God Who now unites these immeasurable variety and manifoldness into one world, it is He Who brought them into existence right from their very inception.

With this first verse, the principle and fundamental truth, the principle and fundamental fact is revealed to us which completely changes the point of view with which we regard the world and ourselves. This single verse would have sufficed to teach us to think of the world, as God’s world, and ourselves as creatures of God, and to prepare us for the demand to recognize this world emanating from Him, and ourselves completely emanating from Him, as God’s holy possessions; and in this world of God’s, and with all our powers belonging to Him, only to fulfil the Will of God. But the Torah is not satisfied just to announce the creation of the world by God in general, by this one verse of the creation. For the whole of this first book telling of the origin of the world, of human history, and of the history of Israel, is meant to be nothing but an introduction to the Laws of God given to Israel. That is why the Torah leads us up to all the individual phenomena of this earthly diversity to teach us to see and honour the forming, law-giving and governing Word of God, not only in general, but in each individual separate kind of being and group of beings. So that we may elevate ourselves to that height of Jewish feeling and Jewish acknowledgement, of which David’s inspired song sings: that, if all beings, in every place of the great kingdom of the world, each one in its own special sphere and in its own state of development obeys the Law of God set for it, then also ברכי נפשי את הי, then we too would obey the Law of God set for us, and in this obedience to God find the whole beatitude of our lives. Our sages teach us further from the fact that the Torah goes to the length of giving us the detailed creation of the world in its separate different spheres with God’s laws and regulations pertaining to each one, that disturbing a single one of these regulations of even the smallest sphere is equally forbidden and punishable as interfering with the whole of God’s laws for the whole of the world; and conversely how the dutiful observance of even the smallest regulation of God in the smallest matter, is equally important and equally rewardable as the keeping of the whole of God’s commandments. “See”, they say, “not by one word of creation did the world with all its manifold diversity spring into existence but בעשרה מאמרות נברא העולם, with ten words of creation was the world created, to make known the punishment that will befall the wicked who disturb the world that was created with ten Sayings, as well as the goodly reward that will be bestowed upon the just who preserve the world that was created with ten Sayings”. (Our sages reckon the creative sentence בראשית ברא as one Saying and it is followed by nine creative Sayings of ויאמר I.L.) — Not only the world as a whole, and the order of its being is God’s world and the order of its existence His Word, but every single creature, every insect, every plant and its order of existence is God’s world and His order. Woe to those that disturb His world! Hail to those that preserve His world! —

V. 2. והארץ. Therefore, the Word of God goes on, והארץ “and this earth”. We have elsewhere recognized in the designation of the earth by the term ארץ quite definitely the producer of a diversity of objects different in form and nature. Hence, this earth, now standing before us in such an abundance of sharply differentiated objects, היתה was once תהו ובהו. It does not say: ויהי הארץ תהו ובהו in which case it would indeed just continue the historic sequence of what was told in the first verse. But והארץ היתה introduces a fresh trend of thought. The first verse shows us our present heaven and our present earth, and proclaims over heaven and earth the great general fact:— It was God Who brought this heaven and this earth into existence in its material and form! The second verse calls our attention again to this our earth and says: “And this earth which we now see in such sharply individualised objects was once תהו ובהו.

We find the root תהה again only in Rabbinic Hebrew where it has the meaning of astonishment, תהי בה ר׳ יוחנן, תהו בה נהרדעי (Eruvin 66, Baba Kama 112 and elsewhere). Hence also to try to recognize something which is still unknown תהי ליה בקנקניה ,בת תיהא (Avoda Zara 72. — Baba bathra 22). It also has the further meaning of regretting, being sorry for something, תוהא על הראשנות (Kidushin 40). It means, accordingly, the unclear, muddled impression which the condition of something makes on us. דהה is probably also related to it, דהה הימנו to describe a weaker, less pronounced shade of colour. According to all this תהו would describe a chaotic condition which would give us the impression of everything being mixed up, and nothing consolidated separately. More difficult is בהו which we only find elsewhere in ביי, an expression of pain in rabbinic Hebrew, possibly also in בי in classic Hebrew, בהו would then designate the chaotic condition as being intolerable, full of contradiction and struggle. תהו designates chaos subjectively, its effect on us, בהו objectively, its actual condition תהו ובהו would be unclear and unseparated, muddled. תהו ובהו would accordingly be the very opposite of that which ארץ expresses as the present condition of the earth. The earth which now produces such a diversity of separate individual forms and kinds of objects was once an indistinct confused entangled mass.

תהום from the root המם (a preliminary state of glowing) ebullition, effervescence, surging, billowing, does not mean the abyss, the deep, but the surging billowing of the waves, turmoil. The earth, which as the end of the verse shows, comprised water too, solid and liquid in this indiscriminate תהו ובהו condition was a confused seething mass. And darkness lay on the turmoil, there was no light to penetrate the mass to awaken the germs slumbering in this mass to individual separate development; ורוח אלקים and the Breath of God, which now penetrates earthly matter and produces life מרחפת על פני המים was only hovering over the waters. Then God spake: Let there be light! ויהי אור and there was light! (The etymology of רוח and מים as well as היה is worked out in Jeshurun vol. VII pp. 474, 436 and 118).

V. 3. אור: — related to עור to be awake, to become or to be receptive to external impressions (hence also skin, the general organ of feeling), sometimes also to awake — אור, light is the awakening element, that awakens all forces to development. The opposite to אור is חשך, which by its relationship to חזק ,עשק ,חשך to be withdrawn, accordingly designates the condition in which beings are not exposed to the awakening influence of light.

V. 4. וירא ה׳ את האור כי טוב, and similarly at the following creations, וירא ה׳ כי טוב, and at the conclusion of all the work of creation: כל אשר עשה והנה טוב מאד וירא ה׳ את, all these expressions at the individual creations and at the end of the whole work of creation are meant, if we understand them rightly, to lay down the great Truth: that not only the coming into existence of things, but also their continuance in existence, is directly dependent on the free Will of God and on His Satisfaction. Once the art of a human inventor has created something, in most cases, its continued existence gets beyond his control. He has created it but it goes on existing by itself; yea, how often does the work grow over the mortal head of the one whose hand made it. Mortals have the power to make new things, they can unchain forces, combine and unite them, but only too often they lack the power to master the work they themselves have created. They lack the power to bridle the forces they have unchained, they lack the magic to dismiss the genii they themselves have called up. The creation surpasses and overwhelms the creator, he is no longer master over his own work. Not so God and His world. The detail and the whole have not only come into existence through His Almighty Will, but it continues in existence only because His Insight finds its continuance good. After its creation He looks at His work and allows it to continue because He is satisfied with it for as long as He is satisfied.

But the construction of the sentence in which the viewing of the first work is described does away with yet another deplorable erroneous idea. It does not say וירא ה׳ כי טוב האור as it says ותרא האשה כי טוב העץ למאכל and in similar sentences, with perhaps one single exception, but כי טוב וירא ה׳ את האור, not God saw that the light was good, but God saw the light, that it was good. That expresses the complete objectivity of the creation towards the creator, the world to God, and thereby opposes all those erroneous thoughts that make the master-worker become absorbed by his work, God by the world, that teach the doctrine of the immanence of God in the world, and draw God down to a world-god, to the soul of the material world, to a force of nature that beyond the world and without the world has no existence. Not so. After He had created the world and the separate constituents of it, “He looked at them”. The work accordingly is external to the Master, God is outside the world. ברא, He brought it into existence, אמר יהי ויהי, He let His Thoughts become materialised — (הגה ,היה ,חיה see above) — not as the body to the soul, not as an animal or plant to its life, as a work to its maker is the relation of the world to God. In everlasting dependence on Him does the work remain. In everlasting independence from His work is He. Only because God does, and for as long as He does, look on His Work and finds it good, does it continue existing.

This mastery of the Creator over His creations, even after they are created, shows itself immediately in His ויבדל ה׳ בין האור ובין החשך, in His setting in order and fixing boundaries between the newly created light and the old darkness. Both are henceforth to rule the world, both to have their uses for the world. Light to awaken everything to individual life and growth, darkness to give opportunity for forces to penetrate and work internally by relaxing from stimulation. Light is not to work unceasingly, both light and darkness receive their kingdoms, and again it is God, the same God Who called “Light” into the darkness, Who intervened, with His Almighty Power of arranging and limiting, between these two greatest and most important contrasts which were henceforth to rule the world; “and God divided the light from the darkness”. As the root of a plant is a child of darkness, the stem, leaf and crowning blossom, a son of the light, so darkness and light, night and day are the father and mother of every organic being. All life germinates in the womb of obscure darkness, everything matures to independence under the rays of light. And this change accompanies us throughout the whole of our existence here below. In our temporary stay on earth we can not bear constant light. When we have used all our forces for twelve hours in the ray of light, working and attempting and accomplishing, we sink back, weary and enervated, into the old darkness, and, sheltered under the motherly wing of Night, imbibe fresh forces to be able to develop a fresh life of light.

בדל is not like כרת ,שבר ,פרד simply dividing, a negative separating one from another, but it implies at the same time a positive allocation, a separate existence, a separate purpose. Thus ערי מקלט, הבדלת ישראל, הבדלת קדש הבדלת פרכת, הבדלת לוים, הבדלת. Related to it is בתולה :בתל, who still has a separate existence, is not yet joined to a husband. Also פתיל ,פתל, threads twisted to a special cord, and צמיד פתיל, a cover that closes in a vessel and separates it from everything round about it (accordingly also from טומאה). Hence also הפתל, to fight with somebody for one’s independence, one’s authority (being somebody of importance) or rather to wrest one’s independence, one’s authority from somebody. In rabbinic Hebrew בטל has mostly lost its positive meaning, though in עשרה בטלנים to designate people who have leisure to attend to communal matters, it retains the positive meaning, more, it is paramount.

V. 5. ויקרא, and God called the light: “Day!” and the darkness He called “Night!” This can not mean simply He gave the name, for the words light and day are by no means identical, but day is the measure of time in which light rules over the earth, and similarly darkness and night. Apart from day and night, the earth, the sea, and heaven we do not find the Creator “calling” anything by name — even Man, of whom it does not say: He formed a creature and called it Adam. In any case where God does call something by a name it always expresses a mission, a calling for the one to be so called, as Abraham, Israel etc. It is accordingly here also to be taken in the pertinent sense of our sages who say: קרייא רחמנא לנהורה ופקדיה אמצוותא דיממא קרייא רחמני לחשכה ופקדיה אמצוותא דלילא “God called to the light and appointed it to the tasks of the day, and God called to the darkness and appointed it to the tasks of the night”. He directed both to their separate provinces. Light to day, יום related to קום, standing up, where everything arises to its own independence (יבם is also related, the one who is called upon להקים שם לאחיו) the time of being erect; darkness to night; לילה, root לול from which we get לולאות dragging along, the time when everything sinks down and the whole world is lying down, and no longer stands there in its own separate outline. The commencement of each of these times is בקר and ערב .ערב where the two conditions begin to mix, and בקר related to פקר ,בגר ,בכר, to be free, independent, where things separate from each other and appear in their own outline, and it is already possible לבקר to distinguish one from the other. But it says ויהי ערב ויהי בקר יום אחד. The complete day beginning with the בקר developing towards completion by the influence of light is the goal, is the טוב which is the purpose of the Creator, to which night, beginning with ערב and achieving its completion by the influence of darkness, is but the preparation, and only when a בקר has succeeded an ערב has the world passed a day of complete existence.

It is significant that here it does not put the וירא ה׳ כי טוב just before the end of the sentence — as it does in the following creations — but places וירא ה׳ את האור כי טוב immediately after the creation of the light before the הבדלה. It is not the הבדלה but the אור, the light and all the organic life and growth through the light which is designated as the טוב, as the real positive aim of the creation. As such, we should have expected the light to have overcome the darkness, to have entirely done away with the old condition of darkness, and a Kingdom of entire light and life to have begun on earth. And in fact such a condition of entire light and life on earth is promised by the mouth of the prophets as the final goal of the development of the world. A condition where, as Is. in 30,26 says: “the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun twice sevenfold that of the light of the seven days” (of the creation!), where (ibid. XXV,8) “God will do away with death for ever and will wipe away tears from every face” where, accordingly, darkness and weariness and death will have disappeared. As God placed light there as the טוב He furnished it with the power to completely overcome the darkness, and it would have immediately done away with the darkness had not that Kingdom of light on earth presupposed a state of moral perfection in humanity which only beckons to us as the crowning point at the end of the centuries, were it not necessary for us, until that time, always again and again to rejuvenate ourselves in the lap of Night for the life of the light. It was for that that God intervened between the light and the darkness and directed the darkness, for the present, still to keep its reign of night with its ever fresh resowing the seeds of life. It was probably with an eye to this position of the כי טוב at the creation of light that our sages made the saying so pregnant with meaning: שגנזו לצדיקים לעתיד לבא (Chagiga 12a).

V. 6. It is difficult to say with any certainty what is to be understood by the מים אשר מעל לרקיע in this verse. We do know, from the song in תהלים CXLVIII, 4, of שמי השמים אשר מעל השמים, which there — if we uderstand the verse correctly — reaches to the utmost limit of a vastness almost beyond our powers of conception. We are first to think of השמים, the whole immeasurable space of the heaven surrounding the earth on all sides with its countless worlds of stars and then to consider this vastness as a mere point against another שמים which is to it as our heaven is to our earth, and then, above this heaven of heavens: מים. (A poetical conception suited to תהלים I.L.). But the words of the Creation which the Torah uses, as we have already indicated, are not meant to be a revelation of hidden matters which really lie beyond the ken of the human mind, but they quickly pass from the one great sentence, that the whole universe, שמים וארץ was created by God, to the sphere of our earthly world, there too, not so much to tell us how everything there came about, but THAT everything there, the whole diversity of the world with its contrasts and the laws to which all of them are subject, was formed, separated, ordered and governed by God the Creator. And so we must look for the מים אשר מעל לרקיע also within the sphere of knowledge of our earthly world. Heaven and earth, light and darkness, day and night, these were the contrasts that the first day showed us being created and ordered by God. Now we are directed to a fresh contrast to waters above and waters below. The waters below which by constantly beating against the dry land not only affect the physical formation and development of the land, but also as rivers, seas and oceans, separating and joining, found and regulate the historical development of the nations of the world; and the waters from above which belong exclusively to the physical demands for the development of all beings. Before God, — so His Word teaches us — separated the dry land from the water, and thus removed the indispensable dissolving element מים from the earth, He raised water up above an darched the vault of the heavens which we see, the רקיע on all sides over the earth. To this vault henceforth the earth sends up its vapour which as clouds from above absorb the water and give it back to the thirsty earth and its thirsty creatures. Just as light was first spread universally penetrating the whole of the globe, and then was confined to light-bearers shining down their rays from the vault of the heavens to the earth, so water too, was removed from the surface of the dry land to be received again from above according to its requirements. The changing wheel of giving and receiving is the picture of the development in which the whole earthly existence is presented to us. Our ancient sages, in the first pages of תענית have already left us their observant remarks (especially on pp. 4 and 9) on rain and clouds. On 9b they have preserved for us a difference of opinion as to whether, according to Reb. Eliezer, the whole formation of rain is brought about by the evaporation of water from the ocean: ממימי אוקיינוס הוא שותה כל העולם כולו, or according to Reb. Joshua, whether the clouds formed by vapour rising from the earth were the sole means for the earth receiving its water from above: כנוד ומקבלין מי מטר מה אני מקיים ואד יעלה מן הארץ מלמד שהעננים מתגברים ועולים לרקיע ופותהין פיהן כל העולם כולו ממים העליונים הוא שותה אלא. No less doubtful is the actual meaning of רקיע. Were the basic meaning to come from רקע, extending, stretching and one could take רקיע to be characterization of the air, as the gaseous expansion in contrast to the denser water and earth, we could then quite easily take רקיע to be the atmosphere which fills the space between the water below and the waters above. The water flows at its lower edge and the vapour rises to its upper stratum where it forms clouds and dispenses rain. The atmosphere rests on water and bears water. But the meaning of “extending” seems only to be a secondary one of the root רקע .רקע occurs elsewhere only as flattening out, stamping down, trampling down some firm matter. It has rather the meaning of beating thin, by which, it is true, in the case of metals, an extension is achieved. Even קרקע from רקע — similarly to כרכב from רכב seems to be the ground trodden firm or flat. According to that רקיע would mean, as it were, the lower surface of the heaven which appears to us as a dome over and about the earth.

V. 7. ויהי כן. And so it became! it became thus, as God willed it; more probably it means, so it became just as we see it now. The condition in which we see it now was not so from all time but only became so at God’s behest.

V. 8. In the same way as God called to light “Day!” and thereby assigned to it its mission for the earth, so did He call to the vault “Heaven!” and thereby gave it its meaning for the earth. The רקיע is the real heaven of the earth. Everything which the earth receives from the heights of the heaven comes through it. Even light it does not receive direct and pure but only through it and broken, and only so is it prepared and ready for its work on earth. For just as יום designates the day in general, but then more specifically that part of the day during which the development of the most essential function of the day occur; as ארץ, earth, designates the whole globe of the world, but then more specifically the dry land, on which the real life on earth develops; so שמים, too, designates in general the whole extra-territorial world which surrounds the earth in space, but more specifically the lower sphere of it which is directed towards the earth, and which appears to it as the container and transmitter of all the influences, gifts, and forces that it receives from the extra-territorial world.

V. 9. קוד .יקוו מים וגו׳ related to גבא a pool (from which the later גבאי ,גבא collecting money, treasurer) געה ,גוה ,גבה ,קפא ,קבע all of which have the meaning of a gathering, a concentration of substance into one point, whether in depth or height or about or on a central point. (This concentration of matter into one point is only brought about by particles of the substance being given an impetus to strive towards the one place. Hence קו a plumb-line. Transposed to human feeling קוה in the Kal, directed towards God, means, to stream with all one’s being towards God, קוי ה׳, to direct one’s whole being towards God; in the Piel with the acc. קויתי ה׳ it means the opposite, to bring something into being directed towards you, to hope and expect that it will come to us, that it will take its whole direction towards us; construed with אל it is the intensified קוי ה׳ .קוה are those whose whole being strive up towards God. קוה אל ה׳ designates the energy which gives the whole being this direction). God spake, that the waters should gather themselves and concentrate towards one place. The energy that is innate in every drop of water to flow from a height towards the level and finally to gather again in a common bed is the realisation of this almighty command of God, יקוו המים which gave water this unlosable mighty urge. יבש .ותראה היבשה is the diametric opposite of מים. This latter (מכך ,מגג ,מיי ,מקק) is the softening, disolving element. יבש (related to כבש ,גוש ,גבש) is that which is rigid, compressed, dry, which offers opposition to dissolution. With this new contrast the play of change of organic life is prepared. All formation of matter occurs in fluid conditions, production as well as reproduction, all moulding to shape and form struggles to firmness, dryness and rigidity; matter germinates in fluid, attains form and shape in solid. ויהי כן: at God’s command, accordingly, did it become so.

V. 10. ויקרא. God appointed the firm terrestrial body that emerged from the waters to be ארץ, the real earth, in which, through which, and on which, all territorial creations are to find their existence. Water, liquid is only the necessary preparatory condition for them. ולמקוה המים קרא ימים, but to the gathering of the water He called out: “Seas!” Do not remain one gathering of the waters, but break into the dry land and gather yourself into various beds to form separate seas. This dividing of the land by the incursion of the ocean into separate countries effected a yet further diversity in the multiformity of the territorial creations, and became the foundation of all the development of nations. So David sings in Ps. 24,2: “The earth and that which fills it belongs to God, also the human world and they that dwell therein. For He founded it on seas and still continuously establishes it on streams.”

וירא ה׳ כי טוב. “God saw that this division was good”, i.e. that it was in accordance with His plan for the world, therefore He allowed it to continue, and therefore it is continuing. At the previous verse the כי טוב is missing, because it was only with this verse that the work of the separation of the waters was completed. Until then it was a division, a variance, a מחלקת, without expressed purpose. But a מחלקת with purpose by which טוב, goodness, is furthered is not only once כי טוב, but when even another מחלקת is added to it — as here on the third day — is even twice כי טוב, because here the purpose of “goodness” is so much to the fore, it could never have attained life without division. This וירא ה׳ כי טוב brings the first division between the waters above and waters below to a conclusion. That this great cycle and exchange — as we wonderingly see it today still woking with its pristine power — that the ocean surrounds the earth, all water rushes to the sea, rises from the ocean to the clouds above and thence pours down again; after it has watered the earth hurries back again to the sea from springs, brooks, streams and rivers, to start the cycle again, and equally so, the sea and land in a constant succession of interchange. All this is not only so because God had once created it so, but because He, after He had created it, still finds it in accordance with His purposes.

V. 11—13. With this eleventh verse we enter the sphere of organic life. We are shown דשא, the plant-world sprouting from the earth, vegetation scattering its seeds, fruit-trees producing fruit, and all, all these countless varied creations, of all sizes, shapes and forms, all governed by the one great law: למינהו ,למינו that each one works solely for its own species, and only allows itself to develop within the appointed narrow sphere of its own kind. And that great pronouncement, so important for this world is said to us: ויאמר ה׳ תדשה הארץ, that is was God, at Whose command the earth produced vegetation, Who pronounced the great למינו-law, the great law of purity of species which governs every tiny plant in its innermost being and in every fibril of its form, and Whose Word of Law still works on and on and is revealed with all its governing force in every plant and every seedling.

Let us now look at the choice of terms used to present the plant-world for our consideration. We have already tried to work out from their etymology what they are meant to express (in Jeshurun VIII p. 4333 et. seq.). דשא (related to דוש, as דרא to דור etc. from which the Chaldean word דשא, the door is derived) we found to designate plant-life in general, forced up from within the earth, and the lower stage of cryptogamia (e.g. ferns, mosses, algae, lichens and fungi, I.L.), they have no stamens and pistils; עשב (related to עזב, let go and placed on their own), the more independent herbaceous plants which are not perennial, are entirely spent in the purpose of להזריע זרע to scatter seed, which die off after forming seed and must always grow afresh from the earth; and finally עץ (on the one hand from עוף, related to אוץ to press on, hasten, and on the other hand from עצה to close) the tree, in which plant life reaches its highest development, perennial plants in which everything works for one purpose, the formation of fruit — עושה פרי and which does עושה פרי, which only once has to grow out of the earth and thereafter is in a similar relation to the fruit, to that which the earth bears to the lower stages of plant life, all of which are אדמה ,פרי האדמה which must always produce them afresh, whereas the fruit of trees are פרי העץ; and זרע: (related to זרח ,זרה, to throw away from oneself, to radiate out) the seed completely disconnected from the earth which the plant strews out of itself and next to itself; and פרי: (from פרח related to פרח ,פדע ,ברח ,ברה ,ברא) the highest perfection of the liberated (פרה to become free I.L.) plant-seed. In all these phenomena we see the plant developing to an ever-increasing degree of freedom.

But it is a freedom without option. Within definitely fixed limits and according to a definitely prescribed form, all its substance and all its forces working so clearly throughout the great variety of plant life, which rules with such mighty infallible power in the tiniest seedling and finest fibre as much as in the giant trees reaching towards the skies, and only allows it to develop with the greatest freedom within the bounds set for it, this law of God which every blade of grass proclaims as loudly as the tallest cedar is called “למינו!” of its species! מין (from מון from which we get תמונה) is the complex of characteristics by which one group of beings keeps itself separate from others in such a manner that, left to itself, it does not unite with them. This separation of species is expressed by תמונה, the form of the species. תמונה is not the individual shape or appearance that separates one individual of a species from another of the same species — for that we have other names, תמונה — תואר ,תבנית is the form of the species in which the essential characteristic of the species is presented which is common to all members of that species. תמונה accordingly, is the fundamental outline which conveys the idea of any special kind of species. Hence also used of the Divine Appearance. The כבוד ה׳ which brings the special Presence of God to the consciousness of the prophets is called תמונת ה׳ יביט ,תמונה, the intimation, the indication of God. לא ראיתם בל תמונה: “You did not see even any indication of a material form”, nothing, זלתי קול naught but sound, a voice. Thus the prohibition לא תעשה לך כל תמונה is much more comprehensive than לא תעשה לך כל פסל. It is to this, the Law of God visibly ruling the whole world of organic life, that our sages refer the Law of God for Israel when it says: כלאים שעטנז לא יעלה עליך, את חקתי תשמרו, חקים שחקקתי לך כבר את חקתי תשמרו בהמתך לא תרביע כלאים שדך לא תזרע כלאים ובגד “observe ye My Laws regarding forbidden mixtures in breeding animals, in agriculture and in clothing. They say: את חקתי תשמרו חקים שחקקתי לך כבר, “observe My Laws, i.e. My Laws that I have expressed at the creation.” For, as here the object, חקתי, precedes the predicate ordering observance, and it does not put it, as it usually does ושמרתם את חקתי, it is not referring here to laws which are only now given, but to such as had long been in existence, and to which now only the command of שמירה is added. Only in one other case does the Torah use the same construction: משפטי תעשו ואת חקתי תשמרו Levit. 16,4. But that again is referring just to laws, the עריות, which, in their deep inner meaning, are in connection with these כלאים-laws. By those laws of nature, of God ruling organic beings, two different species are mutually כלאים, are כלואים, shut up, closed one to the other, do not unite, accouple. But each keeps its reproductive power solely למינו, to its species. Only human caprice forces them to unnatural, that is to say, to prohibited junction. Left to itself, every organic germ belongs even to-day as exclusively to its species as its very first original ancestor did, on whom, for itself and all its descendants, the Creator pronounced His Word of Law: למינו, But the Torah must consider this law which God implanted in the organic world of nature to be of the very highest importance for our human and Jewish calling, for it has interwoven consideration of it in the whole of our life. Not only does it forbid us actual interference with this law by the prohibition of כלאי בהמה and הרכבת אילן, the unnatural crossing of species of plants and animals which are of different species in nature, but in our whole association with the organic world — as sowing and planting, at the use of animals for work, at using materials obtained from animal and vegetable sources for our clothes, and at the food we eat — in כלאי זרעים וכלאי כרם, in הרישה בשור והמור, in שעטנז and in בשר בהלב it teaches us to keep such order that brings to our minds again and again the great law of “keeping species separate”, and its Greater Lawgiver. These constant reminders keep the warning awake in our minds to honour God as the Lawgiver for our matings too, to allow the Law He has given us to rule our forces and urges, and make it the decisive factor for what we do and what we refrain from doing. Although we have the same forces and urges and phases of development in common with animals and plants, are born, feed, grow, age and die, nevertheless God has created us to a special, and indeed higher מין as human beings, and amongst human beings has appointed us to a special מין as Jews, and has written for human beings and Jews the law for their way of life. The Law of God does not begin only with and for the Jews. Already as organic beings we come under the laws of God, we can only attain our special calling which He has given to us also, within the limits He has drawn for us, we too, like all other beings, can only develop our highest individual independence and freedom within the confines of the Divine Law. The whole תורה is nought but the למינו for the Jewish people. The Law which for all unfree creations is expressed in them, and which rules them compulsorily, is proclaimed for man and Jew so that they shall accept it of their own free will, of their own free will allow it to rule over all their forces and urges and deeds. It is just in this free-willed subordination under the Law of God that they bring their higher מין, the higher calling of their species, to a pure and complete accomplishment. Just as God needs the blades of grass and the cedar trees, the ears of corn and the grapes of the vine in His household of this world, and gives each one its law, in the faithful fulfilment of which, each one joyfully lives its appointed life not worrying why it is a blade of grass and not a cedar tree, why corn and not vine, leaving the plan of the world to God, happily and faithfully making its contribution to the whole — in the same way God needs, in His Kingdom of Man, men and Jews, has given to both the calling and the law that is apportioned to each respectively. The great purpose of God is only then fulfilled when each one joyfully and faithfully carries out the law and the calling that God has appointed for him, and in such fulfilment makes his contribution to the whole, which God expects from him.

Of these laws, regulating and guiding the forces and urges of Man, those concerning עריות, sexual life, stand at the head. On their observance the purity and nobility of the specific spiritual and moral character of men is quite especially dependent. And the higher the species rises the more circumscribed does its sexual life become, the narrower become the limits within which the species can and should reproduce itself. בני נח, too, have עריות, but שאר אחוה ונדה are permitted to them. To ישראל, sexual life is already narrowed by these איסורי כרת, the כהנים by the איסורי לאו דכהונה and the כה״ג, in whom the flower of Jewish individuality is to reach its highest perfection, the boundary is drawn even closer by even a בתולה מעמיו יקח אשה כי אם — חייבי עשה. Thus the spiritual and moral heights only blossom from precisely circumscribed sexual life, and chaste morality is the soil in which alone the divinely pure blossom of the human species thrives.

This intimate connection of the pure continuation of the species with the inviolable obedience which the individual has to pay to God’s laws of reproduction may have a deep-reaching implication in our verse. In the orders given for grasses and herbs the למינו-law is not mentioned. For them it only says: תדשא הארץ דשא עשב מזריע זרע. Nevertheless in the fulfilment of the order it says: ותוצא הארץ דשא עשב מזריע זרע למינהו. So the law למינו must have been assumed as self-understood in the command: מזריע זרע תדשא וגו׳ עשב so that the continued existence of the species is essentially dependent on the keeping of its purity, and every non-observance of God’s Law of reproduction digs a grave for the species. Sexual excesses bring about the death of individuals and nations, and the observations of the limits of sexual life drawn by God in the איסורי ביאה for Man and Jew is the fundamental condition for the spiritual and moral ennoblement of the races of men and Jews. The seriousness of these laws of reproduction is apparent in the sterility of hybrid animals (e.g. although an ass and a mare will interbreed, the resulting offspring, a mule, is sterile, although a few cases of fertility have been recorded as exceptions. I.L.). If the history of the Roman soldiery preserved by Tacitus and Pliny contain reports of their wonder at the astounding abundance and wonderful perfection of the fruit in Judea which fell into the hands of their legions as spoil — a fact also confirmed even by the most pronounced sceptics in the traditions contained in Jewish writings — at least it proves that also in the culture of soil and trees, capricious unnatural, i.e. forbidden crossing of, species is not necessary for bringing fruit to greater perfection. That למינו-law, implied in the command מזריע זרע could then be the meaning of the קל וחומר which our sages laid in the mouth of the herbage, and teach us to understand the proclamation of the guardian genius of the world, the שר העולם, who, according to the deep saying of ר׳ חנינה בר פפא, when the herbage first appeared, conforming with the למינו-law without it having been expressly given to them, proclaimed “the future Glory of God on earth, and all the earthly things conforming to the satisfaction of God over His Creation”: יהי כבוד ה׳ לעולם ישמח ה׳ במעשיו! (Chulin 60a). This is a glimpse of that time when men will have learnt from each blade of grass to submit themselves joyfully to the laws of God, when they will have come to the conviction that observation of the laws of morality is neither just a mood nor a sumptuary law, but that it was rather a condition just as necessary for the true existence and the true flourishing of the human race as it is for all other beings. That will be the time when את חקתי תשמרו will be an accomplished fact on earth and the time when ישמח ה׳ במעשיו! This meaning of the third day for the organic purity of the “vegetable” side of human life, for the lawful moral purity of sexual life and of the pleasures of food, may also justify the meaning of the third day, יום ג׳ of the הזאה בג׳ וז׳, for the return to טהרה from a state of טומאה. It is for the “vegetable” life of Man what the seventh is for his “animal” life. Just as the seventh is the consecration of the spirit, the mind, by the recognition of God, and by human work being subordinated to God, so is the third day the consecration of the body, by keeping it within the moral limits of the Law of God. The consecration of the spirit, of the mind, can not be achieved without the consecration of the body, so much so, that on whatever day the first הזאה may have taken place, that day is always reckoned as being the third day, and only from then must four days pass for the הזאה of the seventh to take place.

It is significant that here, too, the command of למינו for the trees is given not to the זרע but to the fruit: עץ פרי עושה פרי למינו אשר זרעו בו. For trees have a double function, to produce fruit for man, and to carry on the species by the seed hidden in the fruit, and it is just to obtain fruit according to his desire that Man is apt to pay no attention to considerations for the species. That is why the Torah gives the warning: although fruit trees serve for your enjoyment, do not forget that the fruit has a duty also to its own species, that the seed for the continuation of the species lies in the fruit, do not allow your longing for the fruit to lead to degenerating the tree for its species.

It goes on to say: אשר זרעו בו על הארץ, a fruit tree that makes fruit for its species, in which its seed is “above the earth”. The first tree was produced by the earth, the seed of future trees is taken away, separated from the earth, matured על הארץ, above the earth, and henceforth the earth itself must receive the seed to develop and dispense it. In a similar way water was at first spread all over the earth, then raised above the earth, to be dispensed again from the heights to the earth. So too, light was at first spread all over the earth then taken away therefrom, bound to light-bearers up obove, to shine down again to the earth. So also seed and the earth. This reciprocal receiving and giving is the model to which the work of the creation led. The whole of life on earth consists of such change and exchange which such separating and detaching begets. One thing is directed to the other not only for receiving but also for giving. The tree requires the earth, but the earth also requires the tree. Everything receives only to give, and everything given returns again to the giver, multiplied, improved for fresh dispensing of blessing.

V. 14.—19. מאור ,אור ,מארת. Until then אור, the light, was spread over the whole of the earth, and ויבדל ה׳, and God with His Almighty power divided light from darkness. Now, after the light had assisted in the production of plants, those real children of light, it was to be bound to a system of bearers of light, and the earth henceforth was to receive its light down from them. מאור, construction like משכן ,מזבח ,מנורה etc. מארת, doubly חסר. The feminine plural written in an incomplete form, or with the predicate in the singular, as חכמות בנתה, always places the conception of plurality in the background, and rather stresses the one abstract conception of the singular which is presented by a plurality of objects. Thus, at the חטאות פנימיות it says ונתן וגו׳ על קרנות מזבח הקטרת the קרנות are written מלא and there אחת מהן מעכבת מתנה, whereas at the חטאות חצוניות it says ונתן על קרנת מזבח העולה the קרנות are written חסר and there it designates the horns of the altar in their general conception, and accordingly ואם נתן מתנה א׳ כפר. Here the singular is doubly stressed. The plural form is incomplete and the verb יהי is in the singular. Thereby the conception of a harmonious unity of the countless light-bearing bodies in the sky is indicated, altogether in their unmeasurable plurality they form one harmonious system. Also inasmuch as אור, the light itself, here חסר, is expressed as מארת, not “full”, our sages take it that it tells us incidentally that the light, as it now appears to us bound to the light-bearers, is not in its original richness and purity, but radiates to us in a lessened power in conformity with our present still imperfect state, cf. what it says above on וירא ה׳ את האור כי טוב. This state of our imperfection surely is shown in nothing more drastically than in the mortality of young children whose early death can only result from the physical and moral imperfection of their parents, and it is understandable accordingly why the אנשי מעמד fasted on the fourth day of the week עליהם אסכרה על התינוקות שלא יעלה. In the following verse והיו למאורת, in which their calling to give the earth its light is expressed, the root אור is “full”, for their calling is in any case completely carried out. The designation מאור for the constellations moreover states that these are not sources of light, but bearers of light. But it is quite specially repeated that it is only ברקיע שמים, in the sky in relation to the earth, that their purpose is to be bearers of light. What they are in themselves, and what other purpose they may have, lies beyond the scope of the considerations which this history of the Creation wishes to explain to us. It only speaks of their influence and purpose for the physical and spiritual earthly world. Hence it speaks especially only of the sun and moon whose effect on the earth is apparent, and adds the stars, ואת הככבים, whose importance for the earth is less recognizable, just supplementarily. For the tendency of the whole is only to tell us that it was God Who created those great luminous bodies in the sky, through whose light the whole physical and spiritual life on earth is ruled, and also all the stars, and that He assigns them their courses and activities. This calling is expressed thus: — “There shall be a system of light-bearers in the firmament of the heavens to make a distinction between day and night”. This great order which regulates the whole life on earth stands in the foreground. Then secondarily it goes on to say: they are also to serve for אתות and מעדים, for ימים and אותות .שנים, signs, מעדים, fixed times (root ועד) would be the finding of the point in space and time on earth by mean of the fixed position and the regular periodic course of the stars and constellations. By their position in the sky, the stars are signs for ascertaining position and measurements in space on earth. By their periodical course in the sky they serve as means for the most accurate fixing of time on earth. Both depend on the assumption of the reliability of the most exact fixing of the position relative to the earth, and the most accurate regulation of the path and course of the heavenly bodies, and we are told that God imparted and directed their regularity in space and time. This purpose for time is further extended by: ולימים לשנים. By the regular path of the heavenly bodies the whole time on earth is divided into מועדים, the days, too, into hours and minutes. But the days are not all equal to one another, and, by the position of the earth towards the sun and moon, form smaller and longer cycles, ימים and שנים are formed; smaller periods: months, and greater ones: years; or ימים periods of days i.e. years, and שנים periods of years i.e. cycles.

We may not, however, lose sight of the fact that elsewhere in חנ״ך the words אות and מועד do not occur in this general astronomic sense, but the meaning of אותות and מעדים is almost exclusively confined to the sphere of intellectual and spiritual human life. אותות are the appearance of such things which are visible to our eyes and lead to thoughts, are to bring about or awaken thoughts. Thus the great deeds of God are אותות, inasmuch as they should awaken thoughts of God’s Almighty Power and of His management of the world. If at the same time they convince, and where possible, are to have an effect on influencing Man’s power of self-will, they are called מופתים (from יפת having the same meaning as פתה, in the Hifil to bring over, to convince). מעדים (from יעד to fix a rendezvous, to fix a place and time for a meeting) festival times which are fixed by God and also by the nation through קידוש החדש, for a meeting with God. The light-giving heavenly bodies serve both for אותות and מעדים. In general they have become אותות for mankind. The view of the starry heavens, the regular phases of the light of the moon, above all the regulated course of the sun regulating the whole of life on earth, have become, as the Psalmist sings, דברים אין אמר ואין, without speech or words, the great sermon preached from above down to mankind. It has impressed the instinctive presentiment deep in the human breast of the existence of some higher power, and proclaims to the whole world: “There is a God!”. They have also served as special אותות, as special tokens of remembrance and signs of God’s promises and decisions. His first promise to mankind, and the first law He gave to Israel, that was to keep Israel always conscious of its own destiny, were perpetuated by God by astronomical writing. He directed newly-re-established mankind on the newly re-presented earth to the rainbow in the sky, and spake: זאת אות ברית “this is the sign of the covenant I have established between Myself and all human flesh on the earth”. When Abraham was to have some idea of the future of his people, God led him out to look at the starry heaven and spake: כה יהיה זרעך, so shall thy seed become, as numerous and as directly pendant on the Mouth of God as the stars. And when Israel was to take its first step in its national, historical and spiritual future — a future so pregnant with conflict and fight — God called its leader out to look at the young crescent of the new moon emerging to light, and spake: “לכם החדש הזה, this renewal of light is your sign, your model”, דוגמה שלכם. Just as up there the moon always struggles out of darkness into light, so are you always to struggle up again out of every darkening of mind and spirit, and out of every dark period of your history, up into fresh purity and clarity, into new life and brilliance. To carry through the world this proclamation of deliverance ever to be found from evil and guilt, of rejuvenation to freedom and life never to be lost, is your mission. כזה ראה וקדש, and as often as the moon shows itself growing to new light, sanctify that time in your national circles to bring about such rising afresh to new light of the mind and spirit, of morals and happiness and life. So the heavenly bodies were to become אותות, signs for mankind and Israel. (and just so that קידוש החדש should not sink down to a mere empty astronomical reckoning of time, apart from, and in addition to such reckoning it was essential ראיה לקדש על פי). ולמעדים, for times appointed by God for Israel, before the Presence of God and in union with His Torah, ever afresh to take to heart the memory of the facts of their redemption and of their being made holy. They, too, are all connected with the revolutions of the moon and the seasons fixed by the course of the sun, everywhere directing Jewish minds at the same time to nature and history to show the same God ruling in the same way over nature and history. This possibility also, to use these אורות ברקיע השמים for אותות ומועדים, for the education of mankind and Israel, is no less dependent on the regular course of these bodies directed by the Creator, and the words interposed, והיו לאותות ולמועדים may indeed well refer to these human historical purposes of the heavenly bodies for mankind and Israel. One need not be surprised to find here already at the history of the creation, as well as at the work of the third day, reference made to matters given later on in the Torah. One must remember that the complete Torah with all the explanations had been taught orally to the people for forty years and the greater part of it practised as part of their daily life, before its main features and the general outline of its history were committed to writing and handed over to them for reference, to ensure the preservation of the complete oral teaching. This is a fact that can not too often be brought and kept in mind for the understanding and correct way of taking the תשב״ב, the “written” Word of God. When this history of the creation was given into the hands of the Jewish people, the מאורות had already become אותות and מועדים According to this, one can also understand how our sages on this verse developed further the idea of the מאור הקטן being symbolic of Israel in its relation to the greater light, symbolic of the other nations who reckon their years by the sun.

V. 20. The creations of the first three days are connected with those of the following three days. The light created on the first day receives bearers on the fourth day, and thereby only then receives completely that position relative to the earth that was necessary for its action in the development of life on earth. The water and air space of the second day received its world of life on the fifth day; and the dry land, created and adorned with vegetation on the third day, received its living inhabitants on the sixth. With the seventh a new world started, the world of the education of Man to God. It was again a first day, but on a higher scale, spiritual light was created, the light of recognition of God. But its fourth day, its bearers are lacking: אין לו בן זוג. Only with the creation of Israel, God’s eighth work for His plan of this world, did this spiritual light, too, receive its bearer, ישראל יהיה בן זוגך as our sages express this relationship.

With the fifth day we enter the sphere of living creatures. To the edge of the ocean the Word of God leads us, shows us water and air and says: God spake: “Let the waters bring forth moving living creatures and let birds fly over the earth before the vault of the heaven”. שרץ (phonetically related to שרש and זרז which also express a vigorous driving movement) seems, by the ץ which expresses a more intensifying, an overcoming of external hinderances, to express independent movement, the first and most obvious sign of life. The tiniest point in which we notice independent movement declares itself, just by that, as being alive. שרץ, accordingly, primarily designates the lower animals whom we specially notice to be alive by their independent motion. But while שרץ refers to independent motion as it appears externally, נפש (related to נפץ to be organically completely separated from the material, see Jeshurun VIII p. 435) is the inner cause of such movement which is innate in every living creature which has an individualising independent life, and which brings about movement (which is why נפש is also used to mean “the will”, for will is nothing else but the starting impulse for a movement). By נפש the creature becomes a self-contained individual, in higher grades, a personality. נפש is something quite apart from the material, it is an intangible something that is innate in every living being and which remains constant in the midst of the ever-changing material body. The mere retention of impressions, memory, which is common to all living creatures, proves the existence of something permanent within the changing material fibres of the body, something which receives and retains impressions. In this נפש lies the specific inner differentiation between animal and plant, just as independent movement is the outer sign. By this נפש the animal has one single centre-point in which its whole existence is concentrated; it dies as soon as this centre-point is destroyed. A plant is not a single whole unit closed round about one centre, one focus. It consists of a number of individual parts boxed together. In every part, every branch, every twig, leaf, and bud, the existence of the whole is repeated, so that, if separated, almost every part can reproduce the whole. The נפש is חיה, is gifted with the power, to test and assimilate that which is homogeneous to it, and equally so, to test and reject, throw out, that which is hererogeneous to it. This free taking in and throwing out of suitable and non-suitable elements is the real activity of living. שרץ נפש חיה, movement, will, assimilating and rejecting, together form the essential signs of life. שרץ: showing life; נפש: the underlying principle of life; חיים: the activity of life, the process of life. — It is doubtful how the ישרצו המים should be taken, whether transitively as in ושרץ היאר צפרדעים or intransitively as in שרץ ארצם צפרדעים. The water shall germinate, or the water shall swarm with etc.

ועוף יעופף. At the creation of the inhabitants of water and air, we do not find the ויהי כן as at the other creations. This may be a confirmation of the correctness of the way we took the כן to refer to the present condition of things which we see before our eyes, (“and thus it became like this as we now see it”. I.L.). Hence we find it said preferably at such creations which form the real habitation of men and so come primarily to his observation.

V. 21. תנינים. A word of doubtful derivation and meaning. Possibly it is the נון with the prefix ת (like תנור from תלמיד ,ניר from למד, perhaps also תפוח from נפח, blown up, ball, apple). נון the Chaldean word for fish may come from the Hebrew נין, offspring, as דג from דגה prolifically increasing, from which we also get דגן wheat, on account of the large number of grains on one stalk. תנין would be a fish, or the whole genus or family of fish. — Here too, in this verse, similarly to the case at זרעים the law of species למינהו ,למינהם is only mentioned when it was actually observed, and at the command, was given as being implied, self-understood.

V. 22. אמר and דבר. There is a fine distinction between the use of these two words, דבר, phonetically related to דור, (the row of contemporary people) טור ,תפר ,תור, means the simple joining of syllables to form words, and words to sentences, thereby to express thoughts in words, without consideration of their entering the ears or affecting the minds of a hearer: simply, speaking. One can speak without a listener. But אמר is to say something to somebody, to convey something to him, related to עומר, the sheaf, חמד, the heap. It connects the words actually spoken with their meaning and purpose, and wants, by means of speech, to bring the concentrated thoughts and undivided will of the speaker to an equal concentration in the mind of the hearer. Hence אמר always has the intention of having an immediate result; not so, דבר. Hence we speak of עשרה מאמרות and עשרת הדברות. God’s words of creation were followed by immediate action. The realisation was the immediate result. God’s words of Law were primarily only the expression of His Will. They remain spoken even if, for the time being, no one listens to them, no one obeys them. Hence we find לאמר everywhere at speeches where the intention is expressed that what is said is to be impressed, understood and its purport completely comprehended. אמר בלבו, to bring something to one’s own mind, to impress oneself with something, or to resolve to do something, and equally so לאמר at a soliloquy where one is one’s own hearer. לאמר at the speeches of God always has the purpose of expressing that the short and precise wording of the speech (וידבר) is to be fully explained and realised in the whole of its sense and purport. It is תורה שבעל פה to the תורה שבכתב. Hence too, the interpreters and explainers of the Torah are called אמוראים. Here at the words of לאמר ,ברכה is used as the other מאמרות of the creation: the fulfilment immediately followed the command. God blessed the organic living creatures, i.e. He gave them the power of reproduction and multiplying, and with this power He gave them at the same time the direction and the urge for it. For in the unfree living organic beings, power and fulfilment are not separated. The power itself automatically drives them to the fulfilment of that for which God has given them that power. It is the Word of God that works on and on in them. Hence it is the blessing of God which speaks on and on in them: Be fruitful and multiply yourselves and fill the water in the seas, but the birds are to multiply themselves on the earth. פרו is the production of progeny; רבו is the care for the young on which the increase, the multiplication depends.

V. 24.—25. Referring to the plants it says: תדשא, “it shall sprout” from the earth, and with all its own characteristic development it still remains bound to its parent body, the earth. Of the water creatures it says: ישרצו המים water producing free moving creatures, but they still remain within the element which produced them. Only when it comes to the living land-creatures does it say: תוצא הארץ, that the earth is to set them outside the earth. Only with them do living organisms attain an ever higher and ever freer independence right up to Man who, even with regards to his origin only belongs to the earth with part of his being. נפש חיה, see above in v. 20. — בהמה, root בום —בהם, like נור — נהר ,בון — כהן et alia. — בום is only found again in במה, where it means, an elevation which serves for raising an object. בהמה, therefore, would be the most apt denomination for those animals, which, already by their nature submit to serve Man, and by such subordination have formed the most important stepping-stone for the spiritual height which Man was to reach. Without oxen to work for him Man would have to harness himself to the plough and waggon, have to do the hardest work and carry the heaviest loads, and his mind, too, would share the weight of physical exhaustion, out of which he would never have been able to raise himself. Inasmuch as Man could yoke oxen to his plough and waggon, and without bodily exertion could let the sheep, that clothed and fed him, graze, his mind remained free for contemplation of heaven and earth, he could use his mind, and think behind his plough, and reflect while he tarried with his flock. Man has to thank בהמה, his sheep and cattle, for his having been able to rise to greater height, they were במתו. In contrast to them are חית הארץ, the חיה, wild animals which, as they do not subordinate themselves to Man’s service, represent the self-contained life, life belonging independently only to itself, רמש האדמה ,רמש .חיים are the small animals that creep on the ground.

V. 26. All other creatures are introduced only with their creation, at Man, creation halts to proclaim to the world which is already created the intention to make a “Man”, an “Adam”. For this “Adam” is to enter the created world as appointed by God to be its ruler and master. This world is prepared for the entrance of its lord. In this sense the plural נעשה might be understood. The use of the “Pluralis Majestatis” with which human sovereigns proclaim their will to their subjects probably has its origin in the idea that the ruler is not issuing orders from the standpoint of his own individual will, in his own personal interests, but that he only looks upon himself as being at one with his people, and the orders and decisions are only made from the point of view of the general interest, and for the general well-being and happiness. It is only as representative of the people that the King rules over them. In the same way the Creator announces to the world the appointment of its master equally in its own interest, out of consideration of the purpose for which it exists. In similar way at the scattering of the people of the world we find הבה נרדה נבלה שם, out of consideration of, for the benefit of, the future of mankind itself. The “Pluralis Majestatis” occurs in the speeches of God in those cases where that, which on the surface appears to be a restricting, disturbing, interference, is meant to be understood as being in reality something which is happiness-bringing, rescuing and necessary. אדם, see Jeshurun VII p. 524 et seq. There we tried to make it clear that both grammatical and logical analogy speak against the usual assumption that the word אדם is derived from אדמה, which would make “earth-born” the characteristic of Man, whereas clearly אדמה is derived from the word אדם. The characteristic of being “earth-born” is one which is common to all animals, and the special characteristic of Man would be just that he is not entirely originated from the earth, but that the breath of God, breathed into his earth-made body made him into a Man. The manner in which a preliminary announcement is made here already tells us that in אדם the creation of a being of a higher nature and a higher calling is about to be made. In sentences like ואתנה צאני צאן מרעיתי אדם אתם the word אדם can not possibly have reference to origin from a block of earth. In the article referred to above we traced the etymology of the word אדם to come from the meaning אדום red, as the leastbroken ray of the spectrum, of the pure ray of light, i.e. the nearest revelation of the divine on earth; from the phonetic relation to הדם, foot-stool, as הדום רגלי שכינה on earth, as transmitter and bearer of the glory of God on earth (in contrast to במה ,במה is the means of raising something or somebody while הדום spares a superior from placing his feet on the earth. Without setting Man to be הדום = אדם, God Himself would have to consummate all the truth, the equity, the benevolence and the love that He wishes to be demanded on earth.
